stimuli.text: A particle moves along the x-axis. Its velocity is given by $$v(t) = 5\sin\left(\frac{t^2}{5}\right) - 0.5$$ for $$0 \leq t \leq 6$$. At time $$t = 0$$ the particle is at position $$x = -3$$.

A particle moves in the xy-plane so that for $$0 \leq t \leq 3$$, $$\frac{dx}{dt} = 4\sin\left(\frac{t^2}{4}\right) + 1.5$$ and $$\frac{dy}{dt} = \cos(t)\,e^{t/4}$$. At $$t = 0$$ the particle is at $$(2, 3)$$.
A particle moves along the x-axis with velocity $$v(t) = 3t^{2} - 18t + 24$$ for $$t \geq 0$$. At time $$t = 0$$ the particle is at $$x = 4$$.
People enter an amusement park at a rate modeled by a differentiable function $$P$$, where $$P(t)$$ is measured in people per minute and $$t$$ is measured in minutes. Selected values are shown.

The function $$f$$ is defined by the power series $$f(x) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^{n+1}x^n}{n\cdot 4^n} = \frac{x}{4} - \frac{x^2}{2\cdot 16} + \frac{x^3}{3\cdot 64} - \cdots$$ for all $$x$$ in its interval of convergence.

questions.stem: What is $$\int_{-1}^{2} \left(6x^{2} + 2x - 2\right)dx$$?

options.why: This is F(b) only; subtract F(a) as well.
This adds F(a) instead of subtracting it.
This subtracts values of the integrand instead of an antiderivative.
Correct. An antiderivative is $$F(x) = 2x^{3} + x^{2} - 2x$$; $$F(2) - F(-1) = 15$$.

questions.explanation: By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, $$\int_{-1}^{2} f(x)\,dx = F(2) - F(-1)$$ with $$F(x) = 2x^{3} + x^{2} - 2x$$. That is $$16 - (1) = 15$$.

questions.stem: What is $$\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\tan(8x)}{3x}$$?

options.why: Correct. Write it as $$\frac{8}{3} \cdot \frac{\tan(8x)}{8x}$$; the second factor approaches 1.
$$\frac{\tan u}{u} \to 1$$ only when the angle and the denominator match. Here they differ by a factor of $$\frac{8}{3}$$.
This inverts the ratio of the coefficients.
Substitution gives $$\frac{0}{0}$$, which is indeterminate, not 0.

questions.explanation: Using $$\lim_{u \to 0} \frac{\tan u}{u} = 1$$ with $$u = 8x$$: $$\frac{\tan(8x)}{3x} = \frac{8}{3} \cdot \frac{\tan(8x)}{8x} \to \frac{8}{3}$$.

questions.stem: What is $$\frac{d}{dx}\left(\cos^{2} x\right)$$?

options.why: Correct. This is the chain rule: the derivative of the outer function, evaluated at the inside, times the derivative of the inside.
This differentiates the inside but then substitutes it incorrectly into the outer derivative.
This leaves out the derivative of the inside function.
This makes a sign or coefficient error in the outer derivative.

questions.explanation: Treat $$\cos^{2} x$$ as a composite and apply the chain rule: $$\frac{d}{dx}\left(\cos^{2} x\right) = -2\cos^{1} x \sin x$$.

questions.stem: $$\int \left(6x^{2} + 2\cdot\frac{1}{x} + 3e^{x}\right)dx =$$

options.why: Correct. Raise the power by one and divide by the new power; the antiderivative of 1/x is ln|x|; e^x is its own antiderivative.
This differentiates instead of antidifferentiating.
After raising the power, divide by the new exponent.
The antiderivative of 1/x is ln|x|, not a power of x.

questions.explanation: Term by term: $$\int 6x^{2}dx = 2x^{3}$$, $$\int \frac{2}{x}dx = 2\ln|x|$$, and $$\int 3e^x dx = 3e^x$$. Add the constant of integration.

questions.stem: What is the sum of $$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} -3\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)^n$$?

options.why: The first term depends on the starting index; check the term for the first value of n.
The formula is $$\frac{a}{1 - r}$$, not $$\frac{a}{1 + r}$$.
Correct. Geometric with first term $$-3$$ and ratio $$-\frac{1}{2}$$.
This divides by $$r$$ instead of $$1 - r$$.

questions.explanation: $$|r| = \left|-\frac{1}{2}\right| < 1$$, so the series converges to $$\frac{-3}{1 - \left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)} = -2$$.

questions.stem: Using the line tangent to $$f(x) = \sqrt{x}$$ at $$x = 9$$, what is the approximation of $$\sqrt{12}$$?

options.why: Sign error: the change in x is added, not subtracted.
The derivative of $$\sqrt{x}$$ is $$\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}$$; this forgets the 2.
This uses slope $$\frac{1}{2}$$ instead of $$f'(9) = \frac{1}{6}$$.

questions.stem: If $$f(x) = \csc x$$, what is $$f'\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)$$?

options.why: This mixes up the derivative with a different trigonometric value at the point.
Check the sign: the derivatives of the co-functions (cot, csc) are negative; tan and sec are not.
This value doesn't come from the correct derivative formula.
Correct. $$f'(x) = -\csc x \cot x$$, evaluated at $$\frac{\pi}{6}$$.

questions.explanation: $$\frac{d}{dx}\left(\csc x\right) = -\csc x \cot x$$. Substituting $$x = \frac{\pi}{6}$$ gives $$-2\sqrt{3}$$.

questions.stem: A particle moves in the plane with $$x'(t) = t$$ and $$y'(t) = \frac{4}{9}t^2$$. What is the speed of the particle at $$t = 3$$?

options.why: Speed is the magnitude of the velocity vector, not the sum of its components.
This forgets the square root.
This is the slope of the path, not the speed.

questions.explanation: At $$t = 3$$, $$\vec{v} = \langle 3, 4 \rangle$$, so the speed is $$\sqrt{9 + 16} = 5$$.

questions.stem: Let $$f(x) = 2x^{3} + 9x^{2} + 12x$$. At what value of $$x$$ does $$f$$ have a relative maximum?

options.why: Correct. $$f'(x) = 6(x + 2)(x + 1)$$ changes from positive to negative at $$x = -2$$.
This is where f″ = 0 (the inflection point), not a critical point.
At this critical point $$f'$$ changes from negative to positive, which gives a relative minimum.
$$f(0) = 0$$, but $$f'(0)$$ is not zero, so this is not a critical point.

questions.explanation: $$f'(x) = 6x^2 + 18x + 12 = 6(x + 2)(x + 1)$$. Testing signs: $$f'$$ is positive left of $$-2$$, negative between $$-2$$ and $$-1$$, positive right of $$-1$$. So there is a relative maximum at $$-2$$ and a relative minimum at $$-1$$.

questions.stem: What is $$\int_0^{\pi} x\sin x\,dx$$?

options.why: Correct. Integration by parts, then evaluate at both limits.
Sign error in the integration-by-parts formula.
This drops the second term produced by integration by parts.
This evaluates only part of the antiderivative or only one limit.

questions.explanation: Use integration by parts: $$\left[-x\cos x + \sin x\right]_0^{\pi} = \pi$$.

questions.stem: A twice-differentiable function $$f$$ satisfies $$f'(4) = 0$$ and $$f''(4) = 0$$. Which of the following must be true?

options.text: $$f$$ has a point of inflection at $$x = 4$$.
options.why: $$x^3$$ has an inflection point there, but $$x^4$$ does not.
$$-x^4$$ has a maximum, but $$x^4$$ has a minimum with the same conditions.

options.text: There is not enough information to classify $$x = 4$$.
options.why: Correct. When f″(c) = 0 the Second Derivative Test is inconclusive: $$x^3$$, $$x^4$$ and $$-x^4$$ all have f′(0) = f″(0) = 0.
$$x^4$$ has a minimum, but $$-x^4$$ has a maximum with the same conditions.

questions.explanation: With $$f''(c) = 0$$ the test gives no conclusion. Use the First Derivative Test instead.

questions.stem: What is the average value of $$f(x) = 3x^{2} + 1$$ on the interval $$[0, 3]$$?

options.why: This is the average rate of change of f, not the average value.
Correct. $$\frac{1}{3}\int_0^{3} f(x)\,dx = \frac{1}{3}\left(30\right)$$.
This is the integral; divide by the length of the interval.
This averages the endpoint values, which only works for linear functions.

questions.stem: What is $$\lim_{x \to 5} \frac{x^{2} + x - 30}{x - 5}$$?

options.why: The expression is undefined at the point, but its outputs nearby approach a single number, so the limit exists.
Substituting gives $$\frac{0}{0}$$, an indeterminate form, not the value 0.
Correct. The numerator factors as $$(x - 5)(x + 6)$$. Cancel $$x - 5$$ and substitute: $$5 - (-6) = 11$$.
This adds the roots. After cancelling, the expression is $$x + 6$$, which approaches $$11$$.

questions.explanation: Direct substitution gives $$\frac{0}{0}$$, so factor: $$x^{2} + x - 30 = (x - 5)(x + 6)$$. For $$x \neq 5$$ the expression equals $$x + 6$$, so the limit is $$5 - (-6) = 11$$.

questions.stem: A curve is defined by $$x = t^{2}$$ and $$y = t^{3} + 4t$$. What is $$\frac{dy}{dx}$$ at $$t = 1$$?

options.why: This is $$\frac{dy}{dt}$$ alone.
This is $$\frac{dx/dt}{dy/dt}$$, upside down.
This divides second derivatives, which is not the slope.
Correct. $$\frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt} = \frac{7}{2}$$.

questions.stem: A population satisfies $$\frac{dP}{dt} = 0.003P(800 - P)$$ with $$P(0) = 200$$. What is $$\lim_{t \to \infty} P(t)$$?

options.why: The population changes from its initial value; it is not constant.
Logistic growth levels off; it does not grow without bound.
Correct. The carrying capacity: the factor $$(800 - P)$$ makes growth stop at $$P = 800$$.
This is where the population grows fastest, not its limit.

questions.explanation: Since $$0 < P(0) < 800$$, $$\frac{dP}{dt} > 0$$ and $$P$$ increases toward the equilibrium $$P = 800$$.

questions.stem: The sum of $$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n}$$ is approximated by its first 8 terms. What is the smallest upper bound on the error given by the alternating series error bound?

options.why: The exponent stays the same as in the series.
This is the last term used, not the first one omitted.
Correct. The error is at most the first omitted term.

questions.explanation: The terms alternate, decrease in size and approach 0, so $$|S - S_{8}| \leq b_{9} = \frac{1}{9}$$.

questions.stem: A function $$f$$ has $$f(2) = -2$$, $$f'(2) = 1$$ and $$f''(2) = 6$$. Using the second-degree Taylor polynomial for $$f$$ about $$x = 2$$, what is the approximation of $$f(2.1)$$?

questions.stem:
Which of the following series converge?

I. $$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \cos\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)$$

II. $$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{2^n}{n!}$$

III. $$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^n$$

options.why: Correct. I: diverges (terms approach 1 (nth term test)). II: converges (ratio test gives L = 0). III: converges (geometric with |r| = 2/3 < 1).
Check each series with an appropriate test: I diverges, II converges, III converges.
Check each series with an appropriate test: I diverges, II converges, III converges.
Check each series with an appropriate test: I diverges, II converges, III converges.

questions.explanation: Series I diverges: terms approach 1 (nth term test). Series II converges: ratio test gives L = 0. Series III converges: geometric with |r| = 2/3 < 1.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the solution to the differential equation $$\frac{dy}{dx} = -2y$$ with initial condition $$y(0) = 4$$?

options.why: Correct. Separating, $$\ln|y| = -2x + C$$, so $$y = Ce^{-2x}$$ and $$C = 4$$.
The exponent must include the growth constant $$-2$$.
At $$x = 0$$ this gives $$e^{4}$$, not $$4$$.
The constant multiplies the exponential; it is not added.

questions.explanation: $$\frac{dy}{y} = -2\,dx$$, so $$\ln|y| = -2x + C$$ and $$y = Ae^{-2x}$$. The initial condition gives $$A = 4$$.

questions.stem: What is the interval of convergence of $$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(x - 2)^n}{n\cdot 5^n}$$?

options.why: Correct. Ratio test gives $$|x - 2| < 5$$; the left endpoint gives an alternating harmonic series (converges), the right endpoint the harmonic series (diverges).
The radius is 5, from the factor $$5^n$$.
The left endpoint gives $$\sum \frac{(-1)^n}{n}$$, which converges.
The endpoints are reversed: the right endpoint gives the divergent harmonic series.

questions.explanation: Ratio: $$\left|\frac{(x - 2)^{n+1}}{(n + 1)5^{n+1}}\cdot\frac{n\,5^n}{(x - 2)^n}\right| \to \frac{|x - 2|}{5}$$, so $$|x - 2| < 5$$. At $$x = 7$$: $$\sum \frac{1}{n}$$ diverges. At $$x = -3$$: $$\sum \frac{(-1)^n}{n}$$ converges.

questions.stem: What is the value of $$\int_{1}^{4} f(x)\,dx$$?

options.why: Correct. Add the areas above the x-axis and subtract the areas below it.

questions.stem: Let $$R$$ be the region enclosed by $$y = x$$ and $$y = x^2$$. Which of the following gives the volume of the solid generated when $$R$$ is revolved about the line $$y = -3$$?

questions.stem: Consider the curve $$x^2 - xy + y^2 = 27$$, for which $$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{y - 2x}{2y - x}$$. At which points on the curve is the tangent line horizontal?

questions.stem: What is the slope of the line tangent to the polar curve $$r = 4 - 2\cos\theta$$ at $$\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}$$?

options.why: This is $$\frac{dr}{d\theta}$$, which is not the slope.

questions.explanation: With $$x = r\cos\theta$$ and $$y = r\sin\theta$$: at $$\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}$$, $$r = 4$$ and $$r' = 2$$. So $$\frac{dy}{d\theta} = r'\sin\theta + r\cos\theta = 2$$ and $$\frac{dx}{d\theta} = r'\cos\theta - r\sin\theta = -4$$; the slope is $$-\frac{1}{2}$$.

questions.stem: A 10-foot ladder leans against a vertical wall. The bottom of the ladder slides away from the wall at a constant rate of 2 feet per second. How fast is the top of the ladder moving, in feet per second, when the bottom is 6 feet from the wall?

options.why: The top slides down, so its rate is negative.
Correct. $$x^2 + y^2 = 100$$ gives $$x\frac{dx}{dt} + y\frac{dy}{dt} = 0$$. With $$x = 6$$, $$y = 8$$, $$\frac{dy}{dt} = -\frac{6(2)}{8}$$.
This swaps the roles of x and y.
The two ends do not move at the same speed; their rates depend on the position.

questions.explanation: Let $$x$$ be the distance from the wall and $$y$$ the height. $$2x x' + 2y y' = 0$$, so $$y' = -\frac{x x'}{y} = -\frac{6 \cdot 2}{8} = -\frac{3}{2}$$ feet per second (the top is moving down).

rubric.criterion: Sets up the trapezoidal sum with unequal widths.

rubric.example: The total number of people who enter the park during the first 12 minutes.

parts.prompt: Must there be a time $$c$$, for $$3 < c < 9$$, such that $$P'(c) = 0$$? Justify your answer.

rubric.criterion: Answers yes, citing the Mean Value Theorem (or Rolle's Theorem) with its conditions.
rubric.example: Yes. $$P$$ is differentiable (so continuous), and $$P(3) = P(9) = 68$$. By the Mean Value Theorem there is a $$c$$ with $$P'(c) = \frac{68 - 68}{6} = 0$$.

parts.prompt: Must there be a time $$t$$, for $$0 < t < 3$$, at which $$P(t) = 51$$? Justify your answer.

rubric.criterion: Answers yes, citing the Intermediate Value Theorem and continuity.
rubric.example: Yes. $$P$$ is continuous, and $$51$$ is between $$P(0) = 34$$ and $$P(3) = 68$$, so the IVT guarantees such a $$t$$.

parts.prompt: Find the interval of convergence of the series. Show the work that leads to your answer.

rubric.example: At $$x = 4$$: $$\sum \frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n}$$ converges (alternating series test). At $$x = -4$$: $$-\sum \frac{1}{n}$$ diverges (harmonic).

parts.prompt: Find the first three nonzero terms and the general term of the Maclaurin series for $$f'(x)$$. Then write $$f'(x)$$ as a rational function.

rubric.criterion: Uses the alternating series error bound with justification.
rubric.example: The series at $$x = 1$$ alternates with terms decreasing to 0, so the error is at most the third term, $$\frac{1}{3\cdot 64} = \frac{1}{192}$$.
